title: Queen Mate
lesson: The most fundamental technique in chess. Walk the enemy king to the edge using your king as a partner: keep the queens a knight-move apart (box shrinking), bring your king up, then deliver mate. Do not stalemate the enemy king — when the king is on the edge, give it room or use the king to cover squares.
keyIdea: Shrink the box a knight-move at a time; your king escorts the enemy king to the edge.

title: Rook Mate
lesson: Harder than the queen mate because the rook cannot cover two ranks at once. Use the "rook cut-off" method: cut the enemy king off along a file or rank, walk your king up, then use waiting rook moves to gain the tempo you need. Beware stalemate when the enemy king reaches the edge.
keyIdea: Cut off a rank, bring the king, use waiting moves when the enemy king approaches the rook.

title: Two Rooks: The Ladder
lesson: Two rooks mate fastest: one rook cuts the rank in front of the enemy king, the other checks and pushes it back, then they "ladder" up the board alternating ranks. No king support is needed — just keep the rooks far from the enemy king so they are never attacked.
keyIdea: Alternate rank cut-offs — the ladder never slips if your rooks stay out of reach.

title: Two Bishops Mate
lesson: The two bishops form a perfect diagonal wall that the enemy king cannot breach. Lock the king against the edge with adjacent diagonal blocks, then bring your king in for the final mate. The trickiest basic mate — take your time and never release the wall.
keyIdea: Build the diagonal wall, push the king to the edge, then escort with the king.

title: Bishop + Knight Mate
lesson: The hardest of the basic mates: the king must be driven to the corner that matches the bishop’s color. Use the W-maneuver to force the king across the board. You get up to 45 moves under the 50-move rule — patience, precision, and the king’s help are everything.
keyIdea: Drive to the corner matching your bishop’s color using the W-maneuver.

title: Pawn Ending: Win the Opposition
lesson: K+P vs K is THE fundamental pawn ending. Your king leads, the pawn supports. Take the direct opposition: when the kings face each other with one square between, the side NOT to move wins the key squares. Black has just been forced to move (that is why it is Black to play) — advance your king to take the opposition and shepherd the pawn home.
keyIdea: King in front of the pawn; take the direct opposition; the defender must give way.

title: Pawn Ending: Hold the Draw
lesson: Same position, but White moves first — so the kings are in opposition with White to move, which means White LOST the opposition. Hold the draw by staying in front of the pawn: mirror the white king’s moves and never leave the key squares d5/d6/e5/e6/d7/e7 area. If White ever steps aside, take the opposition.
keyIdea: Stay in front of the pawn; take the opposition the moment the enemy king steps aside.

title: Lucena: Build the Bridge
lesson: The most important rook ending in chess — if you have a rook pawn on the 7th with your king in front and the enemy rook harassing, you win with the BRIDGE: 1.Kc7! Rc1+ (the rook must check or the pawn queens) 2.Rc4!! — building a bridge on the c-file. If Rxc4+ then 3.Kb6 and the pawn promotes; if the rook stays passive, 3.d8=Q. Practice until the bridge is reflex.
keyIdea: 1.Kc7 Rc1+ 2.Rc4 (the bridge!) — interpose on the check file, then promote.

title: Philidor: The Third-Rank Defense
lesson: The most important DRAWING technique in rook endings. Your rook belongs on the third rank (from your side — here the 6th rank), stopping the enemy king from ever stepping in front of its pawn. Your king stays on e7/f7/d7 zone. When the pawn finally advances past your rook’s rank, swing the rook BEHIND the pawn (to the back) and check the enemy king forever — an endless check = draw.
keyIdea: Rook on the third rank stops the king; once the pawn passes, check from behind forever.

title: Queen vs Pawn on the 7th
lesson: A queen normally beats a rook-pawn on the 7th ONLY if the enemy king is far away. The winning method: first stop the pawn from promoting — control the promotion square with the queen from a distance or pin the pawn with the king nearby. Here Qd2! stops b1=Q dead (if ...b1=Q?? then Qxb1). Then walk your king in and mate. If the defender’s king reaches the queening corner, it is a draw — speed matters.
keyIdea: Control the promotion square from a safe distance, then bring the king.

title: Philidor's Legacy: The Smothered Mate
lesson: The most famous combination in chess. Your knight and queen hunt the king together: check with the queen on the diagonal to force the king into the corner, then plant the knight on f7. When the rook is forced to capture, you give the double check with Nh6+ — the king must retreat — and finally sacrifice the QUEEN on g8 so the rook must take, leaving the king smothered by its own pieces. Knight mate finishes it.
keyIdea: Qg8+!! sacrifice — the rook must capture and its own pieces smother the king.

title: Vancura Defense: Rook-Pawn Draw
lesson: The rook-pawn (a- or h-file) is the drawing pawn — when the defending king reaches the corner, even a queen cannot win. The Vancura defense adds the recipe for the rook: attack the pawn from the SIDE (not from behind), keeping your rook active so the enemy king can never shelter from the checks. Keep your king near the promotion corner and take the pawn if it advances carelessly.
keyIdea: Rook attacks the pawn from the flank; king holds the corner. Draw.

title: The Cut-Off: Winning Rook + Pawn vs Rook
lesson: When the defending king is cut off along a rank or file, the win is straightforward: shield your king from the checks, walk it up beside the pawn, shelter on the squares the enemy rook checks from, and push the pawn. Your own rook does the cutting — keep it on the line that separates the enemy king from the action until the pawn is about to queen.
keyIdea: Cut the king off, shelter from checks, promote.

title: Zugzwang: The Winning Tempo
lesson: With only kings and one pawn, whoever must MOVE first in the key positions loses ground. Here the enemy king is on move: it must give way, and your king outflanks it — one step to a side, forcing the reply, then a step forward. Your pawn stays back exactly long enough to keep the extra tempo. This is the geometry behind every pawn-ending win.
keyIdea: Force the defender to move first; outflank with the king.

title: Queen vs Protected Pawn: The Prison
lesson: A queen alone cannot mate — but here the enemy king is imprisoned by its own pawn. March your king next to the enemy king; the queen keeps cutting off escape squares. Capture the pawn only when it is safe (your king guards the capture square), then convert to the basic queen mate. Watch out for stalemate tricks when the enemy king is cramped against the edge.
keyIdea: Bring the king first; the queen alone imprisons, the king delivers.

title: Pawn Breakthrough
lesson: Three pawns face three pawns, and both kings are far away. The breakthrough works when your side pawns are free of enemy pawns directly in front: sacrifice the middle pawn — the opponent must capture, and the recapture opens the path. Here: push the c-pawn; after the forced captures, your a-pawn runs to the queening square while the enemy king is out of reach.
keyIdea: 1.c6! bxc6 2.b6! — bxc6 is the ONLY capture; a c7 pawn cannot take on c6. Then b6, b7, b8=Q. The mirror 1.b6! cxb6 2.c6! is the same idea from the other side.

title: Opposite Bishops: The Second Passer
lesson: With bishops on opposite colors, a single extra pawn often draws — the defender sacrifices for a permanent blockade. The winning recipe is to create a SECOND passed pawn on the other wing, forcing the defending bishop to abandon one front. Fix the enemy pawns on your bishop color, then penetrate with your king.
keyIdea: Two passed pawns on opposite wings beat one bishop.

title: Queen Endgame: Convert the Extra Pawn
lesson: Queen endgames with an extra pawn are usually winning, but conversion demands precision: activate your queen FIRST (centralize, attack enemy pawns, create threats), only then walk your king in. Simplify to a won queen-vs-pawns race when possible. Beware perpetual check — give your king luft and hide from the checks before pushing the passer.
keyIdea: Queen activity first, king second, then push — and dodge the perpetual.
